newsitem.title: USA: Clinton likely to back compromise air standards.
newsitem.headline: Clinton likely to back compromise air standards.

text.p: President Clinton is expected to back a compromise plan that would impose stricter air quality standards but would ease concerns about its immediate financial impact, senior administration officials said late on Tuesday.

Although no final decision has been made, one senior administration official said Clinton would "like a compromise approach" that embraces many of the ideas offered in November by Carol Browner, head of the environmental protection agency, but also deals with the concerns raised by mayors of cities and the heads of large corporations.

"There's not a final decision, but we're certainly close," said one administration official. "I don't think there is any doubt that a compromise will be approved that hopefully satisfies most people."

Browner's proposal, which would stiffen air quality standards and put many states in violation of the Clean Air Act, has generated an intense debate within the administration and among members of Congress as well as many in the public sector.
Much of the controversy has centred on the costs that would be imposed upon states and communities as well as private industry to deal with the stricter regulations.

Although officials declined to discuss specific details of the compromise favoured by Clinton, several said it was likely the new regulations would be gradual to reduce the need for immediate expenditures.

In San Franciso, the U.S. Conference of Mayors voted on Tuesday to oppose a plan by the Environmental Protection Agency to set strict new limits on smog and soot, saying the proposed standards could jeopardise local economies.

Particular pressure has been building on Vice President Al Gore, who wrote a best-selling book on the need to protect the environment when he was a member of Congress, to push for stricter air standards.

Environmentalists, who have been his supporters in the past, have fired warning shots in recent months that they might balk at backing his plans to run for president in the year 2000 if he backs away from concerns about pollution and other issues.

Officials said Clinton was unlikely to make a final decision on the compromise plan until he has satisfied Gore's concerns. Clinton goes to Nashville, Tenn., on Wednesday to participate in a conference on families being hosted by Gore.

On Thursday, Clinton is slated to address a United Nations conference on the environment. Although he was not expected to discuss the decision on the EPA proposal, he did plan to offer a defence of the U.S. position on greenhouse gases.

During the just concluded summit of the leading industrial nations in Denver, Clinton found himself on the defensive because the United States has not been willing to accept the same strict standards and goals for reducing carbon dioxide that the European Union and other countries advocate.
